claims.text: Stripe reported over 1,000 merged pull requests per week that were entirely produced by Minions, human-reviewed, and contained no human-written code (Part 1, February 9, 2026).
Stripe's count of merged, human-reviewed, Minion-produced PRs containing no human-written code rose to over 1,300 per week (Part 2, February 19, 2026).
Mark Doyle of Stripe reported approximately 3,000 Minion PRs merged per week in a talk published May 26, 2026.
Doyle said about 65% of Minion PRs merged without code changes, while in the other 35% an engineer typically took over and changed something.
Doyle said falling back to the user after the autonomous loop is exhausted happened in less than 1% of cases.
Will Gaybrick said in an August interview with David George that about 7,000 PRs came from Minions the previous week, roughly 30% of PRs that week.

Patrick Collison said one Stripe engineer had more than 600 AI-written PRs merged in H1 with exactly one reverted; he also said incidents per unit time rose slightly while overall reliability was essentially unchanged.

Each Minion run starts in a devbox, an AWS EC2 instance containing source code and development services, the same standardized environment Stripe engineers use and treated as replaceable ('cattle, not pets').
Stripe keeps a warm pool of devboxes targeting readiness in 10 seconds, with repositories cloned, Bazel and type-checking caches warmed, and code-generation services running.
The devbox sandbox is a QA environment with no real user data, no production services, and no arbitrary network egress.
Inside the sandbox the agent runs with full permissions and no confirmation prompts, so a mistake's blast radius is limited to one devbox.
An internal security-control framework prevents destructive actions through MCP tools; its implementation is not described.
Stripe says git-worktree-based parallelization would not scale for its use case; separate environments keep parallel agents from interfering with each other's changes.
Stripe forked Block's goose in late 2024 and adapted it to its LLM infrastructure, prioritizing unattended execution over interactive features.

A blueprint is a workflow-as-code state machine mixing deterministic nodes and agent loops; 'Implement task' and 'Fix CI failures' are agentic, while 'Run configured linters' and 'Push changes' run plain code without an LLM.
Blueprint nodes can restrict tool access, change system prompts, or simplify context for a subtask, and teams can build specialized blueprints such as LLM-assisted migrations.

Rules are scoped to subdirectories or file patterns and attached during filesystem traversal rather than loaded globally, to avoid exhausting the context window; Stripe standardized on Cursor's rule format and syncs rules for Claude Code.

Toolshed, Stripe's centralized internal MCP server, held more than 400 tools in Part 1 and nearly 500 in Part 2; relevant tools are run deterministically over links before a run to prepopulate context.
Minions get a deliberately small curated subset of Toolshed tools, with optional additional thematic groups.

Doyle described an Analyze Prompt agent that gathers the Slack thread and referenced tickets/PRs, then a coding agent, an LLM judge comparing goal to diff, and a diagnostic agent, looping up to about ten times before falling back to the user.
Selected local lints run on each push in under five seconds, and Part 2 says a background daemon precomputing lint heuristics makes push-time lint fixes usually arrive in well under one second.
Stripe has over three million tests; CI runs only the relevant tests for a pushed branch.

The February standard blueprint allows at most two CI rounds: push, apply autofixes, give remaining failures to an agent for one repair attempt, push again, then return the branch to a human; retries are capped because of token, compute and time costs with diminishing returns.

The agent prepares a branch and PR using Stripe's template; the initiating engineer inspects and opens it and requests another engineer's review, while Minions are usually invoked by tagging a Slack app and can run several in parallel.
